Chapter 9: The Paradox of Progress—Technology, Change, and the Persistence of Old Beliefs.
Picture this—a brand new gadget shows up at your door. You can't wait to unbox it. There's that spark, that feeling you're about to step into a brighter, easier future.
But after a few weeks? The thrill is gone. That device ends up on a shelf, and before you know it, you're back to your old routines. It's funny, isn't it? The promise of progress slips away, replaced by the comfort of what you already know.
We often think of technology as the great driver of progress, always pushing us forward. Every new invention is celebrated. It's easy to believe the world is getting better, just because our tools are getting smarter.
But here’s something to pay attention to—technology doesn’t automatically rewrite our deepest beliefs. Even as gadgets evolve, old superstitions, biases, and habits stick around. We might upgrade our devices, but the patterns beneath? They’re stubborn.
Think about a company that invests in the latest software, hoping to supercharge productivity. The team gets trained, everyone’s excited... but pretty soon, people slip back into their usual ways of working. The software gets the blame, but really, it’s about something deeper—a hesitation to let go of what's familiar, a fear of shaking things up.
Most of us don’t realize just how much our relationship with technology is shaped by our habits and expectations. We grab onto new tools, hoping they'll be the fix we need. But often? They just reinforce the same old patterns. The myth of progress is powerful—it makes us believe we’re moving forward, even when we’re standing still.
Here’s where the author nudges us to pause and look past the hype. What problems are these shiny new technologies really solving? What old assumptions are they keeping alive? And maybe most importantly—what possibilities are getting left behind?
By asking these questions, we become more than just consumers. We start to use technology thoughtfully, making choices instead of just following trends.
There’s a great example—a teacher brings tablets into her classroom, hoping to transform the way kids learn. At first, everyone’s excited. But soon, the tablets are just being used for the same routines—taking notes, memorizing facts, taking tests. The tool changed, but the approach? Not so much. It’s a clear sign: true progress takes more than new devices. It takes a new mindset.
That’s the paradox of progress—change is always happening, but it’s just as easy for things to stay the same. Technology can open doors, but it can’t do the tough work of questioning, learning, and growing for us.
So, the real challenge? Use new tools wisely. Stay open to change. And remember, the deepest transformations always start from within.
